title: Tenzo Kyokun - Dogen's Instructions to the Cook
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: In this Soto Zen dharma talk, the teacher encourages participants to let go of needing all the answers and instead embark on a journey of exploration and discussion, just as their founding teacher Norman did. They will be exploring Dogen's work "Moon in a Dewdrop," which offers a unique approach to translating ancient texts into modern English. By embracing this process, we can cultivate mindfulness and awareness in our daily lives, including even the most mundane tasks like cooking, by paying attention to detail and intention.

sentences.text: Good morning, everybody.
We really appreciate that we're here.

Just to acknowledge, there are a lot of other things you could be doing on a beautiful spring weekend, that's for sure: working in the farm or the garden, or going to the [unclear: "kava"] to help support the people who are locked up, playing with your kids, relaxing, all kinds of things we could be doing.
But I think it's good that we're here.
Even as odd as our little tradition is, and Dogen, whom we're going to study a little bit, is hard to understand, we actually need this, I think.
I think it helps.
At least I hope so.
I'm thinking a lot about Norman this morning, our founding teacher, and I'll give a little bit of backstory on this particular event.
At first, all that we did was have our weekly sit, which is not much different than it is now: Wednesday night sit, [unclear: "goes Thursday then"].
And then three times a year in Bellingham and three times a year in Vancouver, Norman would come, or sometimes another teacher in Vancouver, other than Norman.
And we have sesshin.
You know what sesshin looks like: sitting and sitting and sitting and sitting.
And Norman would give a talk.
But it's in sesshin and you're sort of half awake.
The instructions for the formal Dharma talk are really just to treat the words as energy.
Just let them flow through you.
You don't have to remember it or anything like that.
Norman was pretty interested in all kinds of texts and studies and teachings, so he would bring up all kinds of interesting things, but we kept feeling like, oh, we're not quite getting the material.
Maybe that doesn't matter, but we're not quite getting it.
Then I was also thinking about the times I had lived at Green Gulch Farm and Tassajara, and some of us have lived at places like that.
There they have a daily routine with a fair amount of meditation, but also classes and study periods, times when you're studying texts and getting to talk about them.
Of course the formal situation in sesshin is that you don't really get to talk about it, which is a great advantage too.
It's great to not talk to each other, and it's great to talk to each other.
So at one point we were talking to Norman, and we asked whether we could somehow do some version of a class or a study period up here when you're up here.
He said, well, yeah, maybe one at a time.
Once a year would probably be good.
And so we created this hybrid between sesshin and a seminar, or a college class, a study retreat or Dharma seminar.
Norman did that for several years.
Then when he started to cut back a little bit, he said, well, maybe Tim, you should do it now.
I was just reflecting this morning that this has not been very easy for me.
Every time it came around again, I felt underprepared and unworthy, the sorts of things one would feel.
And sometimes that was literally true: I literally didn't have enough time to prepare, with all the things I run around and do.
It feels a little bit better now.
But one time, maybe two or three years ago, it was also Dogen. [unclear: "Camera"], which piece now?
Maybe "Only a Buddha and a Buddha."
Did we do that? [unclear: "Maybe only Buddha and a Buddha"].
Anyway, I was running around like crazy in the mindfulness work.
I had been to Tacoma or somewhere.
No, I'd been to a hotel near Sea-Tac Airport to do a seminar for psychologists at the Washington State Psychology Association meeting.
It was barely the same week.
I know it was the same weekend as [unclear: "the surgery tree in the search"], and the sesshin was Saturday and Sunday, like it is.
The [unclear: "presentation offered invitation at the psychologist"] was on Friday.
So I went with my colleague and did the seminar on Friday afternoon near Sea-Tac.
On the way back, I stopped at a Starbucks with all my books.
I had all my Dogen books with me.
I was drinking lots of coffee and trying to figure out what I was going to say the next day.
This is literally true.
But this morning I was realizing that the other thing Norman was modeling for me, and for all of us, is that you don't have to have it all figured out.
You know what I mean?
When he does talks, and when I do talks, I write it out and think about it pretty carefully.
It's a 30 or 40 minute chunk of time, and you can be pretty organized about that if you have a little time to prepare.
But this is hours of exploration and discussion and texts that need some time.
So I was reflecting this morning that when he would come up to do this kind of seminar on a text, he would have some notes scribbled in the margins and so on.
But he wouldn't have five hours of scripted material ready to go, with all the cross references figured out.
The other day I was also listening to Pema Chödron.
Everybody loves Pema Chödron.
Do you love Pema Chödron?
Everybody loves Pema Chödron.
I was listening to this talk, and she was making all kinds of citations and connections without having looked them up or having them quite straight.
Some of them are actually not exactly right, but it doesn't matter.
It's the spirit of it, right?
And we can always go look it up later.
Yeah, I forgot one of them.
One of them I knew to be wrong, actually, but she was like, I think it's kind of like this.
And I was like, that's right, Pema, but that's okay, that's a good point.
So let's enjoy Dogen and relax about whether we've got it all figured out.
I'll try to lead the charge by not having it all figured out.
And so Dogen: [unclear: "we're all at least one or more of the Wednesday night"].
I've been giving some talks on Dogen.
Has everyone been exposed to Dogen?
I don't want to spend too long on his backstory, because we could be here forever.
But he was a really interesting and deep thinker.
He wrote in lots of different forms, and in his writings he kind of folded together lots of different sensibilities and teachings.

The text we're going to look at today is unusual in that way, because he was riffing on a traditional set of instructions for monastic practice called the Shanyuan Shingui, which means the rules of purity for Chan monasteries, for Chan practice.
So there was a manual.
Dogen read a manual.
And I don't know if that manual was available to him in Japan or if he brought it back from China.
I don't know if that's known or not.
He didn't make a list of what he brought back from China, so nobody really knows.
But he's riffing on that, and then he's inserting all kinds of other material.
In this case he's talking about how to be the cook at the monastery, which, based on his personal experience in China, he found to be a really important practice: the practice of being the head cook.
But then he's inserting koan stories and his feelings and thoughts and little pointers and tips.

He's zooming out to really more philosophical ideas, like we've looked at in Bendowa, and then he's zooming into very particular details about how you should plan the menu and how you should take care of the ingredients.
So it's really a fascinating text in that way.
And all of this is pretty recently available to us in English.
Now there's tons of versions and translations.
The translation I want to hand out now, which I will hand out now, is by a small group of English-speaking scholars.
This is [unclear: "T.
Griffin Folk"], who's called Griff by his friends.
I've met a couple of them, and many of them I've read.
That's like four or five American and Japanese scholars who somehow, that's all they do.
I don't know how their university, you know, I guess the academy lives on.
We still can have people doing interesting and obscure scholastic work.
So this is a translation by him.
What I like about it is that there's a small and growing collection of these more scholarly translations.
I've got to pick it up.
You know you want this one too, it's different than what was on the website.
Yeah, this is different than what I put on the website.
I've changed it.
So have both.
If you were so diligent and downloaded and read it from the website, thank you, congratulations.
And this one's different.
It's the same translator, I just made some additions.
A big set of the first translations were by a Japanese man, an artist really, named Kaz Tanahashi.
Just a little bit more backstory on Dogen studies in the West.
What's interesting about Kaz Tanahashi is, for one thing, he's self-taught.
He didn't go do lots of advanced studies in ancient Japanese or anything like that.
He's a self-taught genius.
The other thing that's interesting about Kaz is that he lived in America a really long time.
He's Japanese, he lived in America a long time, and he lived at San Francisco Zen Center a long time.
And he sort of invented a new way of doing translation.
Maybe it's been done by other people, but he sort of invented it.
He would look at the ancient Japanese and the modern Japanese translations of Dogen, which were made in the 30s and 40s.
They were trying to figure out the weird way that, it's like old English and modern English.
So they did a modern Japanese translation, I think in the 30s and 40s.
Kaz would look at those and write a kind of pidgin English.
Said he important principle five ranks or something like that.
Then he'd collaborate with experienced Americans, teachers and students, and try to work that into meaningful English that somehow touched on the feeling of what they thought Dogen was trying to say.
All Japanese and Chinese is hard to translate into English anyway.
There are so many differences in syntax and style and structure.
But then Dogen's extra tricky, as we'll see.
Anyway, the first book of these came out in 1985.
So that's not that long ago.
It's called Moon in a Dewdrop, and probably this is still a classic and a good book to have.

It's got smatterings of Dogen's work from his set of more philosophical essays, Shobogenzo, and also smatterings of the more practical pieces that Dogen wrote to guide the monastics, including this one, Tenzo Kyokun, Dogen's Instructions to the Cook.
But then also other bits and pieces, like poetry and the times when Dogen gave formal talks.
It's believed that he probably had notes, but he didn't write out his formal talks.
His students would run back to their rooms and try to write them down.
So some of his formal talks are in here.
But I want to just share with you now one of the poems, my favorite.
So it's not all dense stuff.
There's also poetry.
He wrote in multiple different styles of poetry too.
Anyway:
*Awake or asleep in a grass hut, what I pray for is to bring others across before myself.
Although this ignorant self may never become a Buddha, I vow to bring others across because I am a priest.*
Beautiful, huh?
Or you can think, because I am a person, or a student of Dharma.
*Awake or asleep in a grass hut, what I pray for is to bring others across before myself.*
*Although this ignorant self may never become a Buddha, I vow to bring others across because I am a priest.*
So there's his intention in writing all this stuff.
Our hope this weekend is not just of me talking or even just Dogen talking, but of all of us interacting and reflecting.
Not in this morning session, but I think in the afternoon session we'll do something that involves a little bit of writing.
So until then, we'll try to all round up pens, and maybe there's some extra paper around here if you didn't bring a notebook.
Sometimes I manage some sort of weird hands-on experiential stuff.
One time we did sketching and another time we did calligraphy.
We'll see what happens.
The periods are longer, so please don't feel too bound by the usual conventions of Dharma talks.
If you need to move or stand up or stretch, and if something doesn't make any sense, please interrupt me with a question.
I'll try to remember to break out lots of times to discuss and comment.
I don't have the schedule in front of me.
T, would you remind us, or somebody with the schedule?
There's one.
How long do we have right now? 1150.
Okay, so we've got another 55 minutes.
That's great.
All right, so what I've done in this new handout is take Griff's translation and break it into sections.
I made up these sections and I made up the titles of the sections.
This really helps me find my way and stay oriented in the text.
And it's a helpful thing to do for yourself, too.
But in this case, since I got the gig, you get my version, but you can do your own.
You might break it at different places or think of different titles and topics for what he's trying to say.
The original texts in Asian languages usually don't have sections or chapters, and you'd be lucky if they even have punctuation.
It's usually just pages and pages and blocks and blocks of characters, and you figure out in the context of reading it how it's divided and separated.
So this was written by Dogen not too long after he had returned to Japan and was teaching independently, in 1237.
Conveniently, he was born in 1200, so he's 37 years old.
It's probably the third or the fourth major piece of writing that we know about that he did.
Probably lots have been lost, too.
First he wrote a version of Fukanzazengi that we chant here in the morning sometimes.
Then he wrote Bendawa that we looked at, and then some other stuff.
Now he's at his second small temple just outside of Kyoto, the capital.
I guess it would be called Hiei or something like that.
And he's trying to get organized, right?
He's trying to figure out how he wants to organize his monasteries and all this.
This is just a little before he moves to Eiji to really go out in the mountains, so it's a transitional time in his career.
There's lots you can say and guess about his career, and there's lots of theories.
Dogen studies is a whole field.
He's a pretty rich character.
So anyway, let's just start reading.
We're going to get to an interesting koan before too long, which will be a good occasion to break out and discuss.
At first I'll just read out loud, and you can choose whatever your learning style is, if you want to read with your eyes or just listen.
This might be unrealistic, but my vain hope is we'll actually read every word of the whole text.
We might need to skip some stuff towards the end: "Whoops, we're behind."
That's actually a traditional part of Dharma teaching: you spend way too long on the title in the beginning and then you have to rush through the end.
So that's traditional.
Usually, the Tibetans are best at this.
You might have been to a few of these.
The Tibetans really are into text, and they go very carefully through them.
Usually the entire first talk, which is often two or three hours long, is just on the title.
But we'll skip that.
It just means Instructions to the Cook.
So, section one, the overview.
*Buddhist monasteries have in principle six stewards, so six important officers.
All are disciples of Buddha and all carry out the work of Buddha.
Among them is the officer known as the cook, the tenzo, who is in charge of preparing meals for the assembly of monks.
The rules of purity for the [unclear: "chaun"] monasteries, [unclear: "chaun yuan xing yu yi"], says, in order to provide nourishment to the monks of the community, there is a cook.
From ancient times, the position has been assigned to senior monks who have the way-seeking mind, eminent persons who have aroused the thought of awakening.*
*In general, the job of cook is an all-consuming pursuit of the way.
If one lacks the way-seeking mind, it will be nothing but a vain struggle and hardship without benefit in the end.

The rules of purity for [unclear: "chaun"] monasteries says, one should maintain a way-seeking mind, make adjustments in accord with the occasion, and see to it that the great assembly receives what is necessary and is at ease.
In days of yore, monks such as Guishan and Dongshan performed this job, and various other great ancestral teachers did too at some point in their careers.*
*Thus, this is surely not the same as the work of worldly cooks, imperial cooks, and the like.*
So right away, this is worth reflecting on a little bit, I think: that ordinary stuff like being the cook is not ordinary.
The title I ambitiously put on our weekend is Awakening in Everyday Life, or something like that, right?
Everything we do has a depth to it.
It's not just to hire some cook from the village and give them your menu, but to consider it deep spiritual practice.

This next part gets a little bit more personal, because his style of learning about this, which we'll see, was both to read about it and experience it as a student, as a monk enrolled in a big monastery in China, but also to talk to people and really to listen to people: "How do you understand what's going on here?"
So he goes on:
*When this mountain monk, Dogen,*
This is a little bit more literal translation.
When there are square brackets, by convention it means the translator is adding words that weren't actually there, so that it makes more sense.
All Dogen wrote was "this mountain monk," and he means himself.
*Was in Song China, on my days off, I inquired of retired elders of the monks who had held minor and important offices,*
So both minor and important offices.
*and they shared something of their views with me.
Their explanations are the bones and marrow bequeathed by the Buddhas and ancestors, who are possessed of the way in ancient times.
As a rule, once you carefully read the rules of purity for Chan Monasteries, and after that, once you pay heed to the detailed explanations of those retired senior officers.*
So, especially listen to your elders.
And as we'll see quite a bit later, there's a story in here of one of his first encounters with one of these guys, and he comes off as a kind of cocky young thing, and he learns from his elders.

Dogen could also be a, he had lots of different personalities like we all do, and sometimes he comes off as a total know-it-all, kind of hard-ass character, and other times he comes off as quite tender and sweet and humble.
So we'll see both phases of Dogen in this text.
Let's keep plowing on a little bit longer here.
So, section three, the daily routine of the Tenzo.
*First, following the mid-day meal, we're going to get into the details.
Following the mid-day meal, go to the offices of the prior and comptroller, and get the ingredients for the next day's meals, rice, vegetables, and so on.
Having received them, protect and be frugal with them, as if they were your own eyes.
Chan Master Yong of Bao Ning Monastery said, "Protect and be frugal with the monastery property, which is like your own eyes.
Respect and value them as if they were ingredients for an imperial repast."
These cautions apply to fresh and cooked things alike.*
So this is a famous imagery that Dogen brought forward, but he's quoting it from someone else.
What if we were to treat everything like our own, like holding our own eyeballs?
To us that sounds like a really creepy image, but you know what he means, right?
That much tenderness and care with something as fragile and as important as our own eyes.
*Next, the various stewards consult in the store hall,* or does that say stone hall?
Store hall, *about what seasonings should be used on the following day, what vegetables should be eaten, how the rice [unclear: "goals"] should be prepared, and so on.

The rules of purity for Chan Monastery say, "When deciding about ingredients as well as the flavors and numbers of side dishes for meals,"* side dishes, by the way, is like the condiments, *"first consult with the stewards in the store offices."
The stewards referred to here are the prior, comptroller, assistant comptroller, rector, cook, and labor steward.
"When the flavors and numbers have been decided, write them on the announcement boards, in the abbot's quarters, common quarters, and elsewhere."*
By the way, here's another challenge of translation.
The translator has to decide what English words to use for all these Japanese names of offices, and they're Japanese versions of Chinese words too, all the more confusing.
In this case, the rector is the eno, and the other ones are also other kinds of titles, which we may or may not have heard of, because we're quite simplified here from the full meal deal.
But if they translated it as the eno, then anybody not hanging out at the Zen places would say, what the heck is that?
I eno, I know.
Anyway, it doesn't matter too much, but just to know.
Is the labor steward the soku, or?
Ah, soku.
Yeah, probably.
Or we say work leader sometimes.
Soku.
I'm not sure.
But yeah, I'm sure a lot of these, if we heard the Japanese name, we'd recognize them.
If you want to dig into this stuff, Chris, or anybody does, there's another text we have access to, which is a modern Soto church rituals manual.
I have a version of that with both the English versions and the Japanese versions, so we can cross-reference.
I can find it for you.
It's very detailed and very, very boring.
But we should probably break it out and get familiar with it at some point.
It has detailed explanations of every single ceremony that one can do in Zen, but it's always in the context of a big monastery with lots of officers and stuff.
Anyway, the interesting point for us here is that it's a very cooperative, community arrangement.
So the tenzo doesn't just set his menu and go to Safeway, you know.
He receives whatever's available from one officer, and a lot of that's probably donated or grown in the monastery fields.
Then he has to consult with all the other officers: what should I make, what should we eat?
There are lots of rules and guidelines about that.
So there's a constraint on individuality and this great sense of each person taking a lot of responsibility.
The tenzo does a big job, but he or she doesn't just get to do whatever they want either.
*After that, ready the next morning's rice gruel.
When washing rice, preparing vegetables, and so on, do so with your own hands.
With close attention.
Vigorous exertion.
And a sincere mind.
Do not indulge in a single moment of carelessness or laziness.
Do not allow attentiveness to one thing result in overlooking another.
Do not yield a single drop in the ocean of merit.
Even a mountain of good karma can be augmented by a single particle of dust.*
So your mind really matters.
Your mind really matters.

*The rules of purity for the Chan monastery says, "If the six flavors are not provided, then it cannot be said that the cook has served the assembly."* And I wrote down somewhere what the six flavors are.
I'll find that for you.
*When examining the rice, first check for sand.
When examining the sand sifted from the rice, first check for rice.

If you pay careful attention to detail, watching when coming and watching when going, then your mind cannot be scattered and the food will naturally be replete and the three virtues endowed with the six flavors.*
So now he's going to try to explain how to pay attention by citing a Zen story.

Here's the great and confusing thing about our Zen tradition: so much of it is communicated with stories, which don't exactly explain in the conceptual way that our minds would want things to be explained, but challenge us to enter into a kind of mythic space and interact with these different characters.
We were looking at a different Dogen piece yesterday, a group of us, and Chris had a great little point.
She emailed me later, if you don't mind if I share this, that it's like you poke at these stories.
And poking is a lot more productive if there's a group of us poking.
Then sometimes meaning just sort of flows out of it.
I forget how you said it, meaning just sort of emerges.
So it's a little bit like that.
Here's a story about a former cook, about a tenzo.
*When Zhui Feng resided at Dongshan monastery, he served as a cook.
One day when he was sifting rice, Master Dongshan asked him, "Are you sifting the sand and removing the rice, or sifting the rice and removing the sand?"
Zhui Feng said, "Sand and rice are simultaneously removed."
Dongshan asked, "What will the Great Assembly eat?"
Zhui Feng overturned the bowl.
Dongshan said, "In the future you will go and be scrutinized by someone else."*
So let me say a few words, and then what I'm going to do is invite us to break into groups and explore some themes here.
One theme right away here is the theme of sifting.
You might have noticed I gave some words during the first period of zazen, thinking a little about this with you.
There's a way that we're always trying to sift things out, right?
There's stuff in every situation that we like or we don't like, or that is helpful or unhelpful.
And literally here, since the rice came from the rice fields, it wasn't super clean.
Everything's so processed and organized for us.
You buy a bag of rice, you're not worried about getting the sand out of it.
Bags of beans, do bags of beans sometimes still have little stones in them?
Yeah, so maybe bags of beans are that for us still.
It's not reasonable for the farmers and producers to get every tiny little stone out of the bag of beans.
Anyway, we have something in front of us that has this mix.
How are we to interact with that?
Is it a matter of sifting out and removing, pulling out the stuff we like to gather a little pile of the things that we like?
Is it a matter of extracting and removing the things that we don't want to be there, the sand in this case?
Dogen's saying that we need to pay attention.
When we're doing this, we can do it very automatically.
But our hope here as practitioners is to pay more attention to how we do this and what the spirit is that we bring to it.
And is it right to think that the sand is bad and the rice is good?
Xue Feng is the student here in this story.
Deng Shan is, a little confusingly, both the name of the place and the name of the teacher.
Shan means mountain.
The monasteries were usually on some degree of mountain, although the mountains were sometimes not really like beautiful crags like you picture in your mind.
It would be like this place here.
We're on a little slope of Xiom Hill.
That's enough of a mountain.
So if we were a little more traditional, this would be Xiom Mountain Monastery, and you'd call me Xiom from now on.
Then you get this double meaning: "Have you been to Xiom?"
It could refer to the mountain, it could refer to the monastery, it could refer to the teacher, or sort of all three.
We made a great joke about this one time.
Norman gives a retreat every year with Kate and Michael, of Mountain Rain in Vancouver, in a place called Loon Lake.
So one time I was up there and we said we need to call him Loon.
He took that in good spirit, I thought.
I don't know if we really called him that.
We said we should.
But here they're sticking to stuff, so you get kind of lost in the details.
What are they even talking about?
Is Xue Feng just trying to avoid this issue of picking and choosing?
Picking and choosing is a famous Zen theme, right?
It comes from a very famous Zen story from very early in Zen.
These stories are mostly from the 9th and 10th centuries, and into the 11th century, which is a period of China called the Tang Dynasty.
When Dogen was in China, it was in the next dynasty, the Song Dynasty.
So the Song Dynasty people were always thinking about the Tang Dynasty people.
But even before the Tang Dynasty people, the so-called second patriarch of Zen wrote a famous poem that starts out, "The great way has no difficulties.
Just avoid picking and choosing."
So there's always a reference to that whenever there's picking and choosing.
And that's a great guide for life, right?
Our great life is no problem.
Living in this modern world is no problem.
Not a problem at all.
Just avoid picking and choosing.
No problem.
And of course you can't avoid picking and choosing, so already we have this kind of tautology.
As Wei Feng responds to this question, what do you do with this tautology of picking and choosing?
What you like, what you don't like?
Sand?
Rice?
Which way are you going with all this?
We were talking about politics this morning.
Same thing.
On the one hand, we need to somehow stay positive and human and connected in the face of the national political scene.
On the other hand, it's full of really fucked up sand, right?
There are some real problems here.
So Wei Feng said, well, good and bad are simultaneously removed.
Are simultaneously present.
Are simultaneously okay.
And they're moving back and forth between symbolic and literal in interesting ways.
Duan Shan is saying, okay, so you want to get all symbolic about this?
Well, what about lunch?
You're the cook.
Are we eating sand?
Are we eating rice?
What will the assembly eat?
And Wei Feng just took the bowl, which is like a wide kind of bowl or a wide basket where he was moving the sand to one side and the rice to the other side, presumably.
He just took it and dumped it over.
He probably had a lot of other bowls around.
It's not like it was the whole supply.
It was a symbolic act of what?
Of letting go?
So let's reread Dogen's commentary, and then I'm going to invite us to do a little reflection meditation, and then break into groups and see what we can make of all this.
You'll notice that Dogen set this up when he told us the story, and he's going to come back to it many times.
So first, the previous paragraph, the end of section three, right after that quotation.
*When examining the rice, first check for sand.
When examining the sand sifted from the rice, first check for rice.
Pay careful attention to detail, watching when coming and watching when going.
Then your mind cannot be scattered, and the food will naturally be replete with virtues and endowed with flavors.*
Let's not worry about the list right now.
Then he quotes this story.
Let's take a one-minute stretch break first.
I've been sitting here a while already, and you're welcome to do that any time this weekend.
Maybe we'll distract ourselves then, but that's fine too.
Alrighty, let's sit comfortably and settle ourselves for a moment, lowering the gaze or even closing the eyes altogether, if you like, so we can drop into our own heart space.
I want to invite this contemplation of the rice and sand of our lives to our own selves, because it's so easy for us to externalize.
Feel the breath in the body and stay connected to that feeling.
I want to invite you to bring to mind, or just ask the question and breathe with the question: what are some of the things that you appreciate about yourself?
What are some of the things that you appreciate about yourself?
This could be qualities that you exhibit or aspirations you have, values you carry.
It could be actions you take, qualities, just anything.
The invitation here is to let these come to our minds.
The inner critic is never far away, so let her relax a little bit.
Just be curious: what are the qualities and aspects of myself that I appreciate?
Just toss that question out there and listen, with the breathing, to what comes back.
It's like there's a quiet voice somewhere watching you who's going to answer you, if they do.
What are some of the qualities of myself that I appreciate?
What are my good qualities?
Bring curiosity to this, because who knows what we'll think of.
It might not be the usual things we think of.
